title: Proximity Transient Absorption in van der Waals Heterostructures
authors: Neema Rafizadeh, Ting Zheng, Hui Zhao
abstract: Transient absorption spectroscopy is a widely used technique for investigating ultrafast electronic dynamics, where transient optical signals are generally interpreted as arising from excitations within the material hosting the probed optical transition. A distinct form of transient absorption spectroscopy, termed proximity transient absorption (PTA), is demonstrated, in which the probed optical transition and the monitored photoexcited carriers reside in different materials. Using graphene/hBN/WS$_2$ heterostructures, photoexcited carriers in graphene induce a strong transient optical response at the excitonic resonance of a WS$_2$ monolayer through Coulomb screening, even when the two layers remain electronically isolated by an atomically thin hBN spacer. The resulting signal follows the carrier dynamics of graphene rather than those of WS$_2$, demonstrating that the WS$_2$ exciton acts as an optical transducer of electronic processes in a neighboring material. The signal decreases systematically with increasing hBN thickness, confirming its proximity origin while remaining substantial for separations approaching 2 nm. PTA provides a noncontact approach for optically modulating one material using photoexcited carriers in another and enables probing of carrier dynamics in materials that are otherwise difficult to investigate directly. More broadly, PTA establishes a new modality of ultrafast spectroscopy and reveals that transient optical signals in van der Waals heterostructures can originate from excitations residing in spatially separated layers.
summary: This work introduces Proximity Transient Absorption (PTA) spectroscopy to study electronic interactions in van der Waals heterostructures like graphene/hBN/WS2. By exciting carriers in one material, the technique measures the resulting transient optical signal in a neighboring, electronically isolated material. This confirms that the exciton in the probed layer acts as an optical transducer for processes occurring in the pump layer.
main_problem: The study investigates transient optical signals in van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures where the probed optical transition and the photoexcited carriers reside in different, electronically isolated materials.
main_result: Proximity Transient Absorption (PTA) demonstrates that photoexcited carriers in one material (e.g., graphene) can induce a measurable transient optical response at the excitonic resonance of a neighboring, electronically isolated material (e.g., WS2).
method: The technique uses time-resolved transient absorption spectroscopy (pump-probe setup) to measure the differential reflectance ($\Delta R/R_0$) as a function of time delay.
model_or_system: The system studied is the graphene/hBN/WS2 heterostructure, where the atomically thin hBN spacer is crucial for maintaining electronic isolation between the layers.
key_observables: Transient optical signal magnitude ($	ext{A}_{	ext{carrier}}$) at the $	ext{WS}_2$ exciton resonance, carrier lifetime ($	au$), and the systematic decrease of the signal with increasing hBN thickness.
important_parameters: hBN spacer thickness (ranging from few layers to bulk), excitation fluence, and the time delay between pump and probe pulses.
main_assumptions: The electronic isolation is maintained by the hBN spacer, which acts as a large barrier, and the signal is assumed to originate from proximity effects rather than direct electronic coupling.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the PTA setup, PL shifts confirming dielectric screening dependence on hBN thickness, and time-resolved differential reflectance measurements showing the proximity-induced signal decay.
paper_structure: The paper establishes PTA as a new spectroscopic modality, details the $	ext{Gr}/	ext{hBN}/	ext{WS}_2$ system, presents measurements showing the proximity effect dependence on spacer thickness, and discusses the implications for optically modulating separated layers.
why_interesting: PTA provides a noncontact, all-optical method to probe carrier dynamics in spatially separated quantum materials, which is highly relevant for understanding open quantum systems and charge transfer dynamics at interfaces.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic illustration of proximity transient ab- sorption (PTA). (a) Graphene and WS2 monolayers are sep- arated by a thin hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) layer. A pump pulse generates electron–hole pairs in graphene. The resulting carriers induce Coulomb screening across the hBN spacer, modifying the excitonic resonance of the nearby WS2 layer. The transient change in the WS2 optical response is detected by a probe pulse resonant with the exciton transi- tion. (b) Schematic band alignment and optical transitions in the Gr/hBN/WS2 heterostructure.

FIG. 2. Optical microscope images of the samples. (a) A WS2 flake exfoliated onto a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) substrate, containing a large monolayer (1L) region. (b) An hBN flake exfoliated onto a PDMS substrate, containing re- gions of different thicknesses, as labeled, determined from their optical contrast. (c) The Gr/hBN/WS2 heterostruc- ture fabricated by first transferring the hBN flake onto CVD monolayer graphene on a quartz substrate, followed by trans- fer of the 1L WS2 flake. Colored dots indicate the regions with different hBN thicknesses and location and size of laser spots in optical measurements.

FIG. 3. Photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy. The inset shows normalized PL spectra measured from different regions of the heterostructure sample and from a monolayer WS2 sam- ple on quartz. The main panel shows the WS2 PL peak energy as a function of the hBN layer number.

FIG. 4. Proximity transient absorption spectroscopy. (a) Time-resolved differential reflectance of the Gr/1L-hBN/WS2 het- erostructure measured at various probe photon energies, as labeled. The yellow curves are fits to the data (see text). (b) Contributions from carrier-induced transient absorption (Acarrier, solid red squares) and two-photon absorption (ATPA, open red squares) deduced from the fits shown in (a). The PL spectrum is replotted for comparison (shaded area). The values of Acarrier and ATPA obtained from heterostructures with hBN thicknesses of 2L (green), 3L (blue), and 6L (cyan) are also shown. (c) Decay time constants deduced from fits of all four heterostructure samples.

FIG. 5. Time-resolved differential reflectance measured for samples with different hBN thicknesses, with pump and probe photon energies of 1.512 and 2.010 eV, respectively. The yel- low curves are fits to the data using the model described in the text. The inset shows the amplitude of the carrier-induced transient absorption signal as a function of hBN thickness.
